newsitem.title: USA: National Semi has "cautious optimism" about Q3.
newsitem.headline: National Semi has "cautious optimism" about Q3.

text.p: National Semiconductor Corp Chief Executive Officer Brian Halla said the company has "cautious optimism" about its third quarter financial outlook, but he would reserve judgment until after the holidays.

"We'll wait until after Christmas, because traditionally we do have seasonal slumps. We're happy with the strength, but we're not celebrating it yet," Halla told reporters after addressing a Montgomery Securities investor conference here.
He said the company's own book-to-bill is running "on, if not above" the Semiconductor Industry Association's book-to-bill ratio of 1.15 in November.
The industry figure, released Monday, covers the North and South America market and means that for every $100 of semiconductors shipped, $115 in new orders were received.
The book-to-bill ratio has rebounded this fall after dropping below one for most of the year. A ratio above one is considered a healthy indicator for the semiconductor industry.

Halla said in his presentation that the company had limited visibility currently on its fiscal third quarter, but told investors "we've seen strengthening in most of the channels" and said there was reason for "cautious optimism."
"Historically we've always been down in Q3 from Q2 (sequentially)," he said.
Halla said the company has been scheduling employees to work everyday but Christmas in order to meet demand. "With limited visibility, we're going to leave the cork in the bottle."

National Semiconductor posted net income of $29.5 million, or $0.21 a share, on sales of $661.5 million for its second fiscal quarter ended November 24, compared with $79.8 million, or $0.57 a share, on sales of $711.6 million a year ago.
The company's book-to-bill ratio was above 1.1 in the second quarter, and the company has said its customers are entering 1997 with very low inventory levels.
Halla said the company has not seen any "lagging" in personal computer demand, but noted its chips generally are used in higher-performance, multimedia PCs.

Halla said the company expects to complete the spinoff of its Fairchild unit by the end of its fiscal year on May 31, 1997, "if not sooner." Analysts see the unit as a slower growth, lower profit operation.

By contrast to a year ago, when personal computer makers had bloated inventories of chips and a lackluster holiday selling system, National Semiconductor said its customer's inventory levels were favorable at lower levels.
"Our customer's inventory conditions are fairly good for January, and we'll just have to see," said James Foltz, director of financial relations at National Semiconductor.
Asked about Wall Street estimates, Foltz said, "They are certainly good estimates if we're seeing a rising tide."
"I think we're all looking to see what the results of the sell-through of many of our customers's PCs will be in the January time frame," he added.

Montgomery Securities analysts expect the chipmaker to post earnings per share of $0.95 a share in its fiscal year ending on May 31, 1997 and $1.65 a share for the 1998 fiscal year, compared with $1.40 a share last year.
